title: Why a tracking system cannot handle peak season
excerpt: A representative scenario: how the critical flows of a tracking monolith are identified and separated by service boundaries.

children.text: This article describes a representative scenario. It does not describe work with a specific client, and the results it mentions are expected, not achieved.
For most of the year the tracking system works. In peak season, spikes in queries degrade the whole monolith at once, and nobody can see which flow fails first.
Before splitting anything, the flows that generate the most load and the ones the end customer notices were measured. The starting point is a
that prioritizes by impact rather than by the age of the code.
Shipment tracking was separated first, because it was the most queried flow. Each boundary has its own scaling pace and its own metrics, which allows one part to scale without touching the others.
The migration was done in stages, each with a review before the next peak season. The design of each boundary is documented in the

What to expect from this approach
Scalable service boundaries, better observability on the critical flows and less risk before each peak season. These are expectations of the method, not figures from a real case.
